title: Project Plan for a Research and Reporting System Launch
goal: Develop a project plan for launching a new research and reporting system for the organisation's research department, using Claude alongside Google Docs, Lucidspark, Google Sheets, and Jira.
context:
Why this goal - Project planning is a core, recurring part of my role as a Senior Project Manager. Getting it right early avoids problems later, and it is also a goal where I use AI to support my work.

The workflow below generally includes:
Prepare for a planning session with stakeholders: write a short briefing document so stakeholders come to the planning session informed.
Structure the session to be held with the stakeholders: plan an agenda so the meeting captures the right information.
Draft the project plan: turn session outputs into a structured project plan (tasks, owners, timelines).
Confirm the project plan: check the plan with stakeholders before finalising it.
Transfer the plan ready for sprints and delivery: transfer the finalised plan into Jira.

session_goal_achievement.Why or why not: I completed all the steps (although perhaps not to the same full detailed extent as would be the case in the real workplace).

Step 1.step_action: Draft a briefing/planning document to circulate to stakeholders ahead of the planning session, covering project background, objectives, known constraints, and questions stakeholders should come prepared to answer. Use Claude to input and review.

nodes.label: Sketch project background and session notes offline
nodes.detail: Before opening any tool, the participant jots rough notes on background, objectives, and constraints for the workshop pre-read, deciding to let the workshop team surface constraints themselves rather than pre-defining them.

nodes.label: Prompt Claude to draft the workshop pre-read structure
nodes.detail: After a brief connectivity check, the participant asks Claude for a pre-session planning document readable within ten minutes, covering project background, workshop objectives, and stakeholder questions to consider — explicitly excluding constraints for this pass.

nodes.label: Confirm the pre-read document structure
nodes.detail: Claude plays back its understanding of the requested structure (background, workshop objectives, questions for stakeholders, no constraints section) and asks the participant to share the underlying project details so it can draft the document.

nodes.label: Review Claude's response about the pre-read document structure
nodes.detail: The participant reads Claude's playback of the requested structure (a ~10-minute pre-read with background, workshop objectives, and questions for stakeholders, no constraints section) and judges it broadly fine, but holds off on putting it into the document yet, choosing instead to supply the actual content first.

nodes.label: Supply background detail and request formatting polish
nodes.detail: The participant dictates the actual background content (20-year-old outdated system, expiring contract, not fit for purpose, causing research-team issues) and objectives, and asks Claude to bold subheadings, bullet the content below, and polish the phrasing.

nodes.label: Produce formatted draft pre-read document
nodes.detail: Claude creates Research-Reporting-System-Workshop-Preread.md with bolded subheadings and bulleted content, reframing the stakeholder questions as a "Come Prepared to Discuss" section and adding a one-line note that it is a ~10-minute read.

nodes.label: Review Claude's response about formatted draft pre-read document
nodes.detail: The participant reads through the formatted draft pre-read aloud (title, background on the ~20-year-old system and expiring contract, objectives), checking Claude's polished wording against what she dictated, and judges it looks good.

nodes.label: Request numbering of objectives and discussion bullets
nodes.detail: The participant reviews the draft and asks Claude to number the Workshop Objectives list and the Come Prepared to Discuss bullets, while leaving Background bulleted.

nodes.label: Deliver finalized numbered pre-read document
nodes.detail: Claude updates the document so Workshop Objectives and Come Prepared to Discuss are numbered while Background stays bulleted, completing the pre-read.

nodes.label: Review the numbered pre-read and copy it into Google Docs
nodes.detail: The participant reviews the updated document, confirming the Workshop Objectives and Come Prepared to Discuss sections are now numbered (identify key phases, realistic timeline, key activities), considers the pre-read complete, and copies it into Google Docs.

user_response.label: adopt
user_response.reasoning: the request for this pre-read doc start from a2, and a3 a6 a9 are refinement of the pre-read doc, so i only put a9 as the target node

nodes.label: Request a stakeholder email announcing the pre-read
nodes.detail: The participant asks Claude for a short, concise stakeholder email referencing the pre-read document, asking recipients to read it by Wednesday (a ~10-minute read), and to add an appropriate title.

nodes.label: Draft the stakeholder announcement email
nodes.detail: Claude produces a short draft email with the subject line doubling as the title, ready for the participant to insert her name and attach the document.

nodes.label: Review the email draft and paste it into the document
nodes.detail: The participant reviews the drafted email, pastes it into the document for reference, and notes she would normally send it to all relevant stakeholders with the pre-read attached, before moving on to Step 2.

user_response.label: adopt
user_response.reasoning: ask for a email, not a part of the pre-read doc, the user's habbit

Step 2.step_name: Develop a structure for planning / workshop to generate basis of project plan
Step 2.step_action: Draft an agenda and structure on Lucid as well as key questions to ask, discussion topics, and facilitation techniques to surface priorities and risks.

nodes.label: Set up the Lucidspark workshop board
nodes.detail: The participant opens Lucidspark, locates a suitable brainstorming/teamwork template, and begins building the board that will host the session's agenda and structure, adding some initial text and enlarging elements on the board.

nodes.label: Dictate initial agenda items and timings to Claude, then ask to see the agenda so far
nodes.detail: She tells Claude she is drafting a session structure on Lucid and dictates the first agenda items (Welcome & Intro 10 min, Reminder of Objectives 5 min, Reminder of Open Questions 5 min, Gathering Project Phases 15 min), then breaks off ('scrap that') and asks Claude to show what it has so far.

nodes.label: Summarize the agenda drafted so far
nodes.detail: Claude lists the four agenda items captured (Welcome & Intro, Reminder of Objectives, Reminder of Open Questions, Gathering Project Phases) and reports a running total of 35 minutes.

nodes.label: Refine and extend the agenda with remaining items and timings
nodes.detail: The participant renames item four to "Identify Project Phases," adds items for sorting phase items, a break, adding timings, identifying skills needed, and wrap-up/close, then asks Claude for the total duration.

nodes.label: Deliver the completed nine-item agenda with total time
nodes.detail: Claude returns the full nine-step agenda (Welcome & Intro through Wrap Up & Close) and calculates a total session length of 125 minutes (2 hours 5 minutes).

nodes.label: Paste Claude's agenda onto the Lucidspark board
nodes.detail: Accepting the two-hour total ('Okay, fine. Let's do that then'), she pastes Claude's nine-item agenda onto the Lucidspark board as-is, deciding not to bother much with formatting.

user_response.label: adopt
user_response.reasoning: start ask claude about the agenda from b2, and keep refining and adopt b5

nodes.label: Manually build out the board's phase and discussion structure
nodes.detail: With the agenda in place ('We need a structure now'), she hand-builds sections for project phases/work streams (e.g. Discovery, post-live support — debating "phase" vs. "work stream" wording), adds brief explanations of discussion topics and facilitation techniques, and does a final review pass, removing an unneeded item before considering the structure complete.

Step 3.step_action: Draft a full project plan based on the outputs of the planning session. Use Claude to refine.

nodes.label: Plan and prompt Claude to role-play the workshop team
nodes.detail: Plans to have Claude role-play the workshop team to generate example content for the Discovery phase, while completing the remaining exercise manually in a spreadsheet. Asks Claude to identify Discovery work streams, their constituent items, likely durations in the public sector, and required roles or teams.

nodes.label: Generate Discovery work streams, items, duration, and roles
nodes.detail: Claude proposes five Discovery work streams (current-state assessment, stakeholder & user needs analysis, market/vendor scan, requirements gathering, risk & compliance review) with items under each, a likely 6–12 week public-sector duration, and a list of roles/teams needed.

nodes.label: Request shorter items and a trimmed role list
nodes.detail: The participant asks for much shorter, single-line bullets under each work stream and just three key teams/roles instead of the longer list.

nodes.label: Deliver trimmed work-stream items and three key roles
nodes.detail: Claude returns single-line descriptions for each work stream and narrows the roles/teams to Project manager, Business analyst, and Research team representatives.

nodes.label: Populate the Lucid board's Discovery section with Claude's output
nodes.detail: Acting as if the workshop team had filled it in, she transfers Claude's Discovery work streams, items, and roles onto the Lucid board, putting in her own estimate for the phase duration (about six months rather than Claude's 6–12 weeks), and decides one phase is enough to proceed with the remaining steps.

nodes.label: Build the project plan spreadsheet by hand
nodes.detail: Switching to Google Sheets, she manually constructs the plan's timeline (roughly two years overall, starting around 2027), lists the five Discovery work streams with her estimated six-month Discovery phase, and checks the emerging plan against her own rubric of clear phases, owners, milestones, and Jira-readiness.

nodes.label: Ask Claude, again as the team, who should own each work stream
nodes.detail: Noticing the owner column is empty, she quickly returns to Claude and asks who would be the owner of the five work streams.

nodes.label: Suggest an owner for each of the five work streams
nodes.detail: Claude assigns ownership across the five streams based on the earlier roles — business analyst on documentation-heavy streams, project manager on vendor/governance-facing streams, and research team reps on user-needs work.

nodes.label: Enter suggested owners into the project plan
nodes.detail: The participant transcribes Claude's owner suggestions (PM, BA, research reps) into the Owner column of the spreadsheet plan.

user_response.label: adopt
user_response.reasoning: the source node is c1, still the role play thing (as team), adopt c8

Step 4.step_name: Review and validate plan with stakeholders
Step 4.step_action: Get Claude to prepare a review summary of the draft plan highlighting key decisions, open questions, and areas needing sign-off, to circulate to stakeholders for feedback before finalising.

nodes.label: Request a stakeholder email summarizing the plan and Lucid board
nodes.detail: The participant asks Claude to draft an email to senior management accompanying the project plan and a PDF export of the Lucid board, with a summary clear enough that stakeholders would not need to open the underlying documents, asking for review by end of August (with flexibility to flag delays) and noting she will seek board approval next.

nodes.label: Draft the summary review email
nodes.detail: Claude produces a draft summarizing the background and Discovery-phase detail it has visibility into, notes the plan and Lucid board are attached (the latter as optional reference), asks for review by end of August with a flag-if-delayed caveat, and closes with the board-approval note; it flags that only Discovery detail was available and that PDF export is assumed to be done manually.

nodes.label: Review Claude's response about the summary review email
nodes.detail: The participant reads through Claude's draft email against her own checklist (questions, decisions, flags, feedback, headline summary, understandable), finds the summary of the current system and workshop accurate, but decides it still needs more detail before sending.

nodes.label: Request additions and a tone/formatting check
nodes.detail: She asks Claude to add the two-year project timeline and ~10-team resourcing detail to the email body, invite questions, ensure the tone suits senior stakeholders, and remove dashes.

nodes.label: Revise the email with timeline, tone, and formatting fixes
nodes.detail: Claude removes the dashes, adds the two-year timeline and ~10-team resourcing note, appends a line inviting questions before sign-off, and confirms the tone reads as clear and respectful for a senior audience.

nodes.label: Review the finished email and copy it into a new document
nodes.detail: The participant reads through the polished email against her own rubric (clear ask for review/sign-off), then copies it into a new Google Doc, noting she still needs to add a title.

Step 5.step_action: Transfer Excel project plan into a Jira-ready structure. Use Claude?

nodes.label: Review the Step 5 task in the document and set up a basic Jira Scrum board
nodes.detail: The participant reads the Step 5 task description in her document and considers whether she would normally use Claude for this manual-transfer step at all, then quickly creates a bare-bones Jira board, noting she is not spending time polishing its setup.

nodes.label: Ask Claude to generate tasks for five Discovery work streams
nodes.detail: Asks Claude to identify all relevant tasks for the Discovery work streams. After the initial message fails to include the list, supplies the five work streams: current-state assessment, stakeholder and user needs analysis, market/vendor scan, requirements gathering, and risk and compliance review.

nodes.label: Generate a detailed task breakdown for each work stream
nodes.detail: Claude produces multi-item task lists for all five work streams, covering everything from mapping current-system functions to defining requirements and identifying compliance risks.

nodes.label: Review the task breakdown and paste the current-state assessment tasks into the Jira backlog
nodes.detail: She reads Claude's task breakdown, decides these tasks belong in Jira, and pastes the seven current-state assessment tasks into the Jira backlog verbatim as individual work items, before deciding the remaining work streams need shorter lists.

nodes.label: Request a trimmed three-bullet version per work stream
nodes.detail: The participant asks for the tasks under stakeholder & user needs analysis and the remaining work streams to be cut down to three main bullets each.

nodes.label: Deliver trimmed three-bullet task lists
nodes.detail: Claude returns condensed three-bullet task summaries for stakeholder & user needs analysis, market/vendor scan, requirements gathering, and risk & compliance review, leaving current-state assessment unchanged.

nodes.label: Populate the Jira backlog and assign items into sprints
nodes.detail: She manually enters the generated tasks into the Jira backlog as individual work items, then role-plays the PM by moving them into two-week Sprint 1 and Sprint 2 based on her judgment of what should be tackled first, leaving some items in the backlog and assigning an item to herself.

nodes.label: Ask Claude about Jira epics and what this project's epics should be
nodes.detail: After noticing she has no epics set up, the participant asks Claude to remind her what counts as an epic in Jira, what epics would fit this project, and how to add one.

nodes.label: Explain Jira epics and propose phase-based epics
nodes.detail: Claude searches the web for current Jira epic-creation guidance, explains that an epic is a large body of related work broken into stories/tasks/sub-tasks, proposes epics mapped to project phases (Discovery, Design & Requirements, Procurement, Build, Testing, Rollout, Closure) as placeholders, and gives step-by-step instructions for creating one in Jira.

nodes.label: Review the proposed phase-based epics and manually create the five phase-based epics in Jira
nodes.detail: Working directly in Jira's UI, she creates epics for the project's actual five phases — Discovery, Commercial/Contracting, Implementation, Go Live, and Post-Live Support — rather than Claude's generic placeholder list.

nodes.label: Ask Claude for standard descriptions of the five epics
nodes.detail: She gives Claude the five confirmed phase names and asks for standard, definitive descriptions to use as each epic's description text.

nodes.label: Provide standard epic descriptions for each phase
nodes.detail: Claude writes generic but professional descriptions for Discovery, Commercial/Contracting, Implementation, Go Live, and Post Live Support.

nodes.label: Ask Claude to tailor the descriptions to this specific project
nodes.detail: The participant asks Claude to make the epic descriptions more specific to the project where it makes sense.

nodes.label: Deliver project-tailored epic descriptions
nodes.detail: Claude rewrites the descriptions to reference specifics from the project — the ~20-year-old legacy system, the expiring contract, research-team data migration and reporting needs — across all five phase epics.

nodes.label: Enter tailored descriptions and dates into the Jira epics
nodes.detail: She pastes the tailored descriptions into each epic in Jira and sets a start date (Discovery beginning in January), tailoring further as needed.

nodes.label: Manually tag, prioritize, and run mock sprint administration in Jira
nodes.detail: Without further Claude involvement (a deliberate choice, since she says she would not use Claude for this), she tags every task with its epic, owner, and priority, sets statuses including a blocked item with a written blocked-reason note, runs a mock sprint review and stand-up cadence, completes Sprint 1 and starts Sprint 2, adds due dates, and repeats the same tagging/prioritizing pattern into further sprints before wrapping up.

user_response.label: reject
user_response.reasoning: reject general epic provided by claude

Step 1.step_action: Draft a briefing/planning document to circulate to stakeholders ahead of the planning session, covering project background, objectives, known constraints, and questions stakeholders should come prepared to answer. Use Claude to input and review.

At least 3 pre-session questions are included for stakeholders to consider
Document is concise enough to be read in under 10 minutes

Step 4.step_name: Review and validate plan with stakeholders

Any questions or decisions requiring stakeholder input are flagged
Feedback deadline and process are clearly stated
Summary is understandable without needing to open the full Excel plan
Tone is appropriate for a senior stakeholder/sponsor audience

Dates and owners are added where possible
